items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Birmingham, AL
items.meta: Own coal, coalbed methane, or oil and gas minerals near Birmingham, AL? Get a hedged, activity-based cash offer confirmed against county probate records.

sections.html:
Birmingham was built on Red Mountain iron ore and the coal seams of the Warrior field, and that history is precisely why so many Jefferson County families discover a mineral interest buried in an old estate file decades after the mines themselves went quiet.

Iron, coal, and limestone drew industry to Birmingham in the late 1800s, and the mineral acquisitions that followed were sweeping, sometimes covering entire sections of land bought or leased from farm families for a fraction of what the minerals would later be worth. When the Black Warrior Basin's coalbed methane boom arrived in the 1980s, some of those same old coal reservations became gas assets, and heirs who had never thought about mineral rights suddenly had a royalty check to explain, or a lease offer to weigh, or, more often, neither.

The Alabama acquisition desk buys mineral and royalty interests from Birmingham-area owners at every stage: fresh inheritances just discovered in a probate file, older interests with a documented royalty history, and non-participating interests where the owner never had leasing rights at all.

sections.title: Layers of mineral history under Jefferson County
sections.html:
It's routine for a Birmingham-area mineral title to show more than one severance: an original coal or iron reservation from a mining company a century ago, followed by a later coalbed methane lease covering the same coal seams for gas rather than solid mineral extraction. Untangling which company, estate, or family holds which layer is often the real work before an offer can be made.

Jefferson County's probate court, which sits in Birmingham itself, is the practical starting point for that work. Between deed records, wills, and prior lease filings, most ownership questions here can be traced, even when the current owner's only clue is an old royalty check or a line on a property tax bill.

sections.title: Where CBM activity concentrated relative to the city
sections.html:
The Black Warrior Basin's most productive coalbed methane fields, including Oak Grove, Cedar Cove, and the broader Brookwood trend, sit primarily southwest of Birmingham toward Tuscaloosa County, with Jefferson County itself hosting a mix of core and flank acreage depending on the specific area. A tract closer to the city's urban core is typically valued differently than one in Jefferson County's less-developed southwestern reaches.

The Alabama acquisition desk checks current well control and permit activity against the specific location of a Birmingham-area tract before quoting anything, since blanket citywide numbers don't hold up well against how uneven CBM development actually was across the county.

sections.title: Heirs, estates, and small fractional interests
sections.html:
A large share of Birmingham mineral interests today are small fractional shares, the result of an original reservation dividing among children, then grandchildren, over three or four generations. It's common for a single heir to hold something like a sixteenth or thirty-second interest, often without realizing any co-owners exist elsewhere.

The Alabama acquisition desk buys interests at that scale regularly. Once your fractional share is confirmed against the county's probate and deed records, the Alabama acquisition desk quotes a range built for that specific percentage rather than requiring you to first coordinate with every other heir.

sections.title: What determines value on a Birmingham-area interest
sections.html:
For coalbed methane interests, the Alabama acquisition desk looks at whether a well is currently producing on the relevant unit, how that well's output has trended, and how comparable interests in the surrounding field have recently sold or leased. For interests with no production history, the range is built from lease bonus comparables and permit activity in the surrounding area instead.

The Alabama acquisition desk won't quote a flat per-acre number sight unseen, and any figure the Alabama acquisition desk does give is hedged against current activity, since Black Warrior CBM production has declined meaningfully from its 1990s peak and continues to shift with commodity prices.

faqs.q: you found an old royalty statement in your grandparents' papers but haven't received anything in years. What does that mean?
faqs.a: It likely means the well that generated those payments has slowed or stopped producing, which is common as Black Warrior CBM wells age. The Alabama acquisition desk can check the current status of that specific well and quote based on where things stand today.

faqs.q: How do you find out if you is one of several heirs to a Birmingham mineral interest?
faqs.a: Jefferson County probate records usually show how an interest was divided among heirs over time. The Alabama acquisition desk helps trace that history and confirm your specific share as part of the offer process.

faqs.q: Is your interest coal, coalbed methane, or oil and gas, and does it matter?
faqs.a: It can matter quite a bit, since a coal reservation and a later gas lease on the same seam are sometimes held by different owners. The Alabama acquisition desk reviews the deed language and lease history to confirm exactly what you hold before quoting.

faqs.q: Do you buy interests with no current production?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Birmingham-area interests the Alabama acquisition desk buys have no active well at all, and the Alabama acquisition desk prices those against lease and permit comparables in the surrounding trend rather than a production record.

faqs.q: What's the difference between selling your mineral rights and leasing them?
faqs.a: A lease is a temporary right to explore and produce in exchange for royalties if a company succeeds; selling transfers the mineral ownership itself for a lump sum now. The Alabama acquisition desk is glad to walk through the tradeoff.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Tuscaloosa, AL
items.meta: Own mineral rights in or around Tuscaloosa, AL? The Alabama acquisition desk evaluates parcels near the Oak Grove and Brookwood coalbed methane fields and make a written cash offer.

sections.html:
Tuscaloosa is the county seat and sits closest of any city in the county to the productive core of the Black Warrior Basin, which puts real weight behind a well-documented mineral interest here.

As the Tuscaloosa County seat, the city holds the courthouse and probate records for every deed and mineral severance filed in the county, which makes it the natural starting point for title work even when the parcel itself sits well outside city limits. Tuscaloosa is also close enough to the Oak Grove and Brookwood coalbed methane fields, the two fields most associated with productive Black Warrior CBM development, that owners here often hold interests with an actual production history rather than pure speculation.

Whether your interest was severed from University-area land, a family farm on the edge of the city, or acreage bought purely for its minerals, the same first step applies: confirm what you hold and where it sits relative to active units before deciding what it's worth.

sections.title: Proximity to Oak Grove and Brookwood
sections.html:
The Oak Grove and Brookwood fields, both just south and west of the city, were among the most productive coalbed methane developments in the entire basin during the 1990s and 2000s, targeting the Mary Lee and Pratt coal groups at depths shallow enough to make degasification economical. Parcels within or adjacent to those field boundaries carry meaningfully different value than acreage on the far side of the county, and the Alabama acquisition desk checks your legal description against the historic and current unit maps before quoting anything.

If your interest has ever produced, even modestly, the Alabama acquisition desk will look at the decline curve on the specific well or unit rather than assuming a flat basin-wide average, since CBM wells in this part of the county have varied widely in how long they've held a plateau before declining.

sections.title: University growth and old family severances
sections.html:
The University of Alabama's expansion and the general growth of the city over the past several decades has pulled a lot of formerly rural land into development, and in many of those transactions the mineral rights were reserved separately from the surface sale. If your family sold land near Tuscaloosa going back a generation or two, it's worth checking whether that reservation survived, because it often did even when nobody involved remembers it explicitly.

The Alabama acquisition desk also sees interests that trace to University-adjacent land companies from decades past. Those chains can be more complex to trace, but they're routine work for the Tuscaloosa County Probate Court records, and the Alabama acquisition desk handles that research as part of the Alabama acquisition desk's review.

sections.title: How the Alabama acquisition desk prices Tuscaloosa-area interests
sections.html:
For producing interests near Oak Grove or Brookwood, the Alabama acquisition desk weigh recent royalty history, remaining reserves as best they can be estimated from public production data, and how the specific well has performed against typical basin decline patterns. For non-producing acreage further from the core, the Alabama acquisition desk prices against comparable Tuscaloosa County transfers and general trend direction rather than a promised royalty stream.

Either way, you'll get a written offer with the reasoning laid out, so you can compare it against a lease bonus, a competing purchase offer, or simply the option of holding the interest as it stands.

faqs.q: How close does your parcel need to be to Oak Grove or Brookwood to have real value?
faqs.a: There's no hard cutoff. The Alabama acquisition desk checks your specific legal description against current and historic unit boundaries and let that determine the answer, rather than relying on distance alone.

faqs.q: your family's records reference a land company that doesn't seem to exist anymore. Can you still trace it?
faqs.a: Yes. Old land company severances are common in Tuscaloosa County, and the Alabama acquisition desk is experienced tracing chains of title through successor entities and the county probate records.

faqs.q: Is a mineral interest near the University campus itself likely to have value?
faqs.a: Developed, densely built areas near campus rarely see new drilling activity, so those interests are typically valued on historic production or speculative basis rather than current development potential, and the Alabama acquisition desk will tell you clearly which applies to your parcel.

faqs.q: What Tuscaloosa County records do you check before making an offer?
faqs.a: The Alabama acquisition desk reviews the probate court's deed and mineral records, current state oil and gas permits, and any producing unit filings tied to your legal description before the Alabama acquisition desk quotes a price.

A mineral interest connected to Mobile rarely sits under the city itself — more often it's tied to family land out toward Citronelle, Chunchula, or the rural western part of the county, held by a family whose home has been in Mobile for generations. Because so much of the original land grant history here predates the standard American township-and-range survey system, tracing a legal description back to its source sometimes means working through old Spanish or French grant boundaries before the deed record even starts looking familiar.

The Alabama acquisition desk has done this kind of research before, and the Alabama acquisition desk does it the Alabama acquisition desk rather than asking a family to hire a surveyor before the Alabama acquisition desk will talk.

sections.title: What the Alabama acquisition desk looks At Before Naming a Number

The Alabama acquisition desk prices against that specific, current information rather than the reputation of Mobile County as an oil-producing area generally.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Tuscaloosa County, AL
items.meta: Own coalbed methane or oil and gas mineral rights in Tuscaloosa County, AL? The Alabama acquisition desk evaluates Oak Grove and Brookwood field parcels and make a written cash offer.

sections.html:
Tuscaloosa County sits at the productive heart of the Black Warrior Basin's coalbed methane development, and that history shapes almost every mineral conversation the Alabama acquisition desk has with owners here.

Tuscaloosa County, with the city of Tuscaloosa as its county seat, was ground zero for one of the country's earliest large-scale coalbed methane plays. Starting in the 1980s and accelerating through the 1990s and 2000s, operators drilled hundreds of wells into the shallow Mary Lee, Pratt, and Black Creek coal seams around communities like Brookwood, Oak Grove, and Vance, producing methane that had previously just been a hazard to underground coal mining. That history means Tuscaloosa County has more genuinely producing mineral interests, and a longer paper trail behind them, than almost anywhere else in Alabama.

It also means ownership here can be complicated. Many tracts were leased and unitized decades ago, passed through several generations of heirs since, and now sit as small fractional interests spread across family members who may not even know each other. The Alabama acquisition desk works through that complexity regularly, whether your interest is a single clean deed or a fraction inherited three generations back.

sections.title: Oak Grove, Brookwood, and the coal seam gas legacy
sections.html:
The Oak Grove and Brookwood fields remain the two names most associated with Tuscaloosa County coalbed methane, targeting coal seams often less than two thousand feet deep, shallow enough that development costs stayed manageable even as prices moved. Wells here typically ramped up production over the first year or two as water was pumped off the coal to release trapped gas, held a plateau, and then declined gradually, a pattern distinct from conventional oil and gas wells and one that matters when the Alabama acquisition desk is pricing a producing royalty interest.

Operators active in the basin's build-out included names like Taurus Exploration and later independents that consolidated leaseholds as the play matured, and many current units trace their unitization orders back to filings from that era. If your family's interest has been part of one of these units for decades, there's usually a documented production history the Alabama acquisition desk can review directly rather than estimate.

sections.title: How title fractures across generations here
sections.html:
Because so much of the county's mineral estate was severed from the surface before the coalbed methane boom even started, often through farm and timberland sales going back to the early 1900s, ownership has had a long time to fracture. A single original 80-acre severance can, after three or four generations of inheritance without a formal partition, end up split among a dozen or more living heirs, each holding a small fractional interest that individually looks negligible but collectively represents real value.

Alabama's intestate succession and heirs' property rules mean that when someone dies without a will, or with a will that isn't formally probated, the mineral interest can pass by operation of law to multiple descendants automatically, sometimes without anyone filing paperwork that clearly documents the new ownership. Tuscaloosa County Probate Court records, along with any producing operator's division order, are usually the fastest way to reconstruct exactly who owns what today.

If you and your relatives jointly inherited a mineral interest and have never formally sorted out the shares, that's an extremely common starting point for the Alabama acquisition desk, not an obstacle. The Alabama acquisition desk can work with the group as a whole, help identify what needs to be documented, and structure a purchase that accounts for everyone's actual share.

sections.title: Understanding a coalbed methane royalty check
sections.html:
Owners with a producing interest sometimes find their royalty statements confusing, since CBM wells report both gas volume and, in many cases, water production, and post-production costs can be deducted before the net royalty is calculated. The Alabama acquisition desk is glad to walk through an actual statement with you and explain what the numbers mean before you decide whether selling makes sense.

Because coalbed methane wells decline in a fairly predictable pattern once past their initial plateau, a producing interest's value depends heavily on how far along that curve the specific well sits, current gas prices, and how many years of economic production likely remain. The Alabama acquisition desk builds the Alabama acquisition desk's offers around that analysis rather than a flat multiple of your most recent check, and the Alabama acquisition desk will explain the assumptions behind the number.

sections.title: What to gather before you call
sections.html:
The single most useful document is your deed or the division order from the operator paying your royalty, since either one will typically show your net mineral acres or your decimal interest in the producing unit. If you're working from an inheritance and don't have formal paperwork, the deceased relative's name, approximate date of death, and county of the property are usually enough for the Alabama acquisition desk to start tracing the chain through probate.

From there, the Alabama acquisition desk confirms your interest, check it against current well and unit records, and return a written offer with the reasoning laid out, whether your tract is squarely inside a producing CBM unit or sits on undeveloped acreage elsewhere in the county.

faqs.q: What makes Tuscaloosa County different from other Alabama counties for mineral owners?
faqs.a: It sits at the core of the historic Black Warrior Basin coalbed methane play, so a larger share of interests here have an actual multi-decade production history compared to counties where minerals are mostly undeveloped or speculative.

faqs.q: your royalty checks have gotten smaller every year. Is that normal?
faqs.a: Yes, coalbed methane wells generally decline gradually after an initial production plateau, so a shrinking check over time is typical rather than a sign something is wrong, though the Alabama acquisition desk is happy to review your specific statement.

faqs.q: you only own a small fraction of an interest that's split among several cousins. Is it worth selling?
faqs.a: Small fractional interests are common in this county given how many estates have passed through multiple generations, and the Alabama acquisition desk buys and price these regularly, whether individually or as part of a group of heirs.

faqs.q: How do you value acreage that's never produced anything?
faqs.a: The Alabama acquisition desk prices undeveloped Tuscaloosa County acreage against comparable recent transfers and its position relative to the active fairway, always as a range tied to current market activity rather than a fixed promise.

faqs.q: Do you need a lawyer to sell your mineral rights?
faqs.a: It's not required, but for interests with multiple heirs or unclear title the Alabama acquisition desk often recommend involving a local attorney, and the Alabama acquisition desk is happy to work alongside whoever you bring in.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Walker County, AL
items.meta: Own coal, coalbed methane, or mineral rights in Walker County, AL? The Alabama acquisition desk evaluates parcels tied to the Black Warrior Basin's deep coal mining history and make a cash offer.

sections.html:
Walker County has produced coal, and later coalbed methane, longer than almost anywhere else in Alabama, and that layered history is exactly what makes valuing a mineral interest here more nuanced than a simple lease price.

Centered on Jasper as county seat, Walker County was one of Alabama's most productive coal-mining counties for well over a century, with underground mines working the Black Creek, Mary Lee, and Pratt coal groups long before anyone thought to capture the methane those seams released as a hazard. When coalbed methane development took off across the Black Warrior Basin in the 1980s and 1990s, Walker County's already-known coal geology made it a natural target, and towns like Jasper, Nauvoo, Cordova, Carbon Hill, Dora, and Parrish all sit within or near areas that have seen coal, gas, or both pulled from beneath them.

That dual history is exactly why title and mineral ownership in this county can be more layered than elsewhere. A single tract might carry a coal lease from one era, a separate gas lease from another, and an inheritance that split ownership across a family sometime in between. The Alabama acquisition desk is used to untangling that, and the Alabama acquisition desk starts every Walker County review by figuring out precisely what rights you hold and under what agreements.

sections.title: Coal, gas, and the difference it makes
sections.html:
In a lot of Walker County deeds, the coal rights and the oil and gas rights were severed at different times, sometimes decades apart, which means it's entirely possible to own the gas rights under a tract without owning the coal, or the reverse. This matters enormously for valuation: a coalbed methane royalty interest is priced on gas production and decline, while a coal royalty, where it still exists as an active or historical interest, follows an entirely different structure tied to tonnage mined.

Before the Alabama acquisition desk quotes anything, the Alabama acquisition desk identifies exactly which estate your deed covers. If your paperwork references both coal and gas, or is ambiguous about which minerals were reserved, that's worth resolving carefully rather than assuming, since it directly changes what a buyer should pay.

sections.title: Underground mining and CBM degasification
sections.html:
A distinctive feature of Walker County's gas history is degasification drilling tied directly to underground coal mining, where operators drilled wells ahead of mining to remove methane and reduce explosion risk in the mines themselves, sometimes selling that captured gas commercially and sometimes simply venting it as a safety measure. Later, as standalone coalbed methane development matured, some of these same coal seams were developed purely for gas production independent of any mining operation.

If your family's interest has a production history going back several decades, it may reflect this earlier degasification-era activity rather than a more conventional CBM lease, and the royalty terms and calculation methods from that era can differ from what's standard today. The Alabama acquisition desk reviews the actual lease and division order language rather than assuming a modern structure applies.

sections.title: Fractionated ownership across mining-era families
sections.html:
Walker County's coal boom brought generations of families into land ownership through homesteads, company-town arrangements, and small farm purchases, and much of that land has passed through inheritance multiple times since without formal partition. It's common for the Alabama acquisition desk to find a Walker County mineral interest split among ten, fifteen, or more living heirs, each holding a small fraction that individually seems too minor to matter but adds up to a meaningful interest collectively.

Alabama's probate process governs how these interests pass, and when a will was never filed or an estate was never formally closed, reconstructing current ownership requires working through the Walker County Probate Court records in Jasper. The Alabama acquisition desk does this regularly and can usually identify the current fractional breakdown from the original owner's name and approximate date of death.

sections.title: What the Alabama acquisition desk looks for before making an offer
sections.html:
For producing interests, whether coal or gas, the Alabama acquisition desk reviews the actual royalty history and current production trend rather than a single recent statement, since Walker County wells and mines have widely varying histories depending on which coal seam and which era of development they belong to. For non-producing acreage, the Alabama acquisition desk prices against comparable recent county transfers and the tract's position relative to historically productive areas around Jasper, Cordova, Carbon Hill, Dora, and Nauvoo.

Whatever the Alabama acquisition desk finds, the Alabama acquisition desk put the Alabama acquisition desk's reasoning in writing alongside the offer itself, so you or your family can weigh it against a competing lease, a pending inheritance decision, or simply the choice to keep holding the interest as it stands today.

faqs.q: Do you own the coal rights, the gas rights, or both under your Walker County land?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on your specific chain of title, since these estates were often severed separately and at different times. The Alabama acquisition desk reviews your deed to determine exactly what you hold before pricing anything.

faqs.q: your family's interest has old paperwork mentioning coal mine gas, not a modern CBM lease. What does that mean?
faqs.a: That likely reflects the county's earlier degasification-era drilling tied to underground coal mining, which can carry different royalty terms than a standard modern lease. The Alabama acquisition desk reviews the actual document to determine how it works.

faqs.q: There are a dozen or more of you who inherited a share of this land. Can you still make this work?
faqs.a: Yes, highly fractionated ownership is common in Walker County given its long mining history, and the Alabama acquisition desk regularly works with large groups of heirs to reach a coordinated purchase.

faqs.q: Is coal royalty valued the same way as gas royalty?
faqs.a: No, coal royalties are typically tied to tonnage mined while gas royalties are tied to production volume and pricing, so the Alabama acquisition desk evaluates each using the structure that actually applies to your interest.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Jefferson County, AL
items.meta: Own mineral or royalty rights in Jefferson County, Alabama? The Alabama acquisition desk buys Black Warrior Basin coalbed methane interests with a clear, patient, honest offer.

sections.html:
Jefferson County sits inside the Black Warrior Basin's coalbed methane fairway, and few counties in Alabama carry as long or as layered a mineral-ownership history, coal, iron, steel, and now natural gas, all stacked on the same land over more than a century.

If you hold a mineral or royalty interest connected to Jefferson County, from Birmingham's old industrial core out to the smaller communities like Fairfield, Gardendale, Hueytown, or McCalla, you are sitting on a piece of one of the most heavily documented, and heavily severed, mineral estates in the state. The Alabama acquisition desk buys these interests, and the Alabama acquisition desk approaches every one of them the way a family office would look at any other asset: understand it fully, weigh a lump sum against the after-tax present value of what remains, and only move forward when the numbers and your goals actually line up.

This page is meant to give you a real picture of what owning minerals in this county typically involves, not a sales pitch.

sections.title: How this county's mineral estate got so fractured
sections.html:
Jefferson County's coal, iron ore, and later natural gas history means the same parcel of land was often leased, mined, sold, and re-leased multiple times across different eras and by different industries. Coal companies acquired large tracts in the late 1800s and early 1900s, then subdivided or sold off surface rights over the decades while various mineral rights stayed reserved in the chain of title. When coalbed methane development picked up in the 1980s and 1990s, operators went back through this same layered history to lease the gas rights specifically, sometimes from the coal-era mineral owner, sometimes from an heir several generations removed from whoever originally struck the deal.

The result is a county where a huge number of owners hold small fractional interests, an eighth, a sixteenth, a sixty-fourth, split among cousins who may not even know each other, all tracing back to one original tract. If that describes your situation, it is the norm here, not the exception.

sections.title: The Black Warrior Basin coalbed methane picture
sections.html:
The core of Alabama's coalbed methane production sits in the Pottsville coal measures, the same Mary Lee, Blue Creek, and Pratt coal groups that were mined underground for generations before operators realized the methane trapped in those seams could be produced on its own. Western Jefferson County, along the Tuscaloosa County line near McCalla and Holt, sits closer to some of the basin's more established producing units, while the county's eastern and southern suburbs, Leeds, Hoover, Homewood, generally sit further from active development.

Energen Resources was historically the dominant operator across much of this coalbed methane fairway. Diversified Energy acquired that legacy portfolio and now operates a large share of the older, mature wells across Jefferson County, meaning many owners today receive statements from a company name that did not exist when the original lease was signed. That is normal, not a sign anything has gone wrong with your title.

These wells are mostly well past their peak. Coalbed methane production in this basin tends to decline gradually rather than sharply, which means owners often see small, steady checks for many years rather than a dramatic payout followed by a cliff. That steadiness is exactly why converting the remaining stream into one lump sum is worth evaluating for owners who have a specific use for the cash today.

sections.title: Probate, heirs, and clearing title in Jefferson County
sections.html:
Jefferson County is unusual in Alabama in that it operates two probate court divisions, one based in Birmingham and one in Bessemer, depending on where in the county the estate was originally opened. If you inherited a mineral interest and are not sure which division holds the relevant file, that is one of the first things the Alabama acquisition desk helps owners sort out.

Because so many of these interests have passed through two, three, or even four generations without formal estate administration at every step, heirs' property situations are common here. You may co-own an undivided interest with siblings, cousins, or more distant relatives you have never met, some of whom may not even know the interest exists. The Alabama acquisition desk can buy your specific undivided share without requiring every co-owner to participate, and where a family wants to sell together, the Alabama acquisition desk can coordinate that too.

In cases where title has never been formally cleared through probate, an heirship affidavit is often enough to establish your ownership without a lengthy court process, though every situation is different and the Alabama acquisition desk will tell you honestly what your specific case requires before you spend time or money on it.

sections.title: What actually drives value for a Jefferson County interest
sections.html:
The Alabama acquisition desk weigh current or recent production against your net decimal interest, the maturity and decline stage of the specific well or unit, and how close your tract sits to active development versus the county's quieter edges. Two interests of identical acreage can be worth meaningfully different amounts depending on these factors, so the Alabama acquisition desk never quotes off acreage alone.

Value talk in this business should always be hedged against real, current numbers rather than promises. What your interest is worth today depends on recent royalty statements, current natural gas prices, and how the specific well is performing, and any honest buyer will tell you that up front rather than quote a fixed price before looking at your documentation.

faqs.q: How do you know which town or unit your Jefferson County interest is tied to?
faqs.a: The legal description on your deed or division order, section, township, and range, tells the Alabama acquisition desk exactly where your interest sits, and the Alabama acquisition desk can trace that against current well and unit records for you.

faqs.q: your statements come from Diversified Energy but your grandparent's paperwork mentions Energen. What happened?
faqs.a: Diversified Energy acquired Energen's Black Warrior Basin coalbed methane portfolio, so this is a normal operator transition that does not affect your underlying ownership.

faqs.q: Do you need to go through probate before you can sell?
faqs.a: If the interest passed through an estate that was never formally administered, you will likely need to clear that first, sometimes through full probate and sometimes through a simpler heirship affidavit depending on your circumstances.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the Birmingham and Bessemer probate divisions?
faqs.a: Jefferson County splits probate jurisdiction geographically, so which division holds your family's estate file depends on where in the county the property or the deceased owner was located.

faqs.q: Can multiple heirs sell their shares separately?
faqs.a: Yes, each heir can sell their own undivided interest independently, and the Alabama acquisition desk regularly works with families where only some members choose to sell right away.

faqs.q: Should you talk to a CPA before selling?
faqs.a: It is worth understanding the tax treatment of a mineral sale versus continued royalty income for your specific situation, and the Alabama acquisition desk would encourage you to run the numbers past your own CPA or tax advisor as part of deciding what is right for you.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Mobile County, AL
items.meta: Own mineral or royalty interests in Mobile County, home of the Citronelle Field? Get a courthouse-researched offer from a family-office buyer, no pressure.

sections.html:
Mobile County has produced oil since 1955, when the Citronelle Field came in as the largest onshore discovery in Alabama history, and the paperwork behind that production has been splitting through estates ever since.

Mobile County is unusual among Alabama counties in that most mineral owners here don't have to be told their ground has history — they already know it, at least in outline. The Citronelle Field, discovered in the mid-1950s in the Rankin and Donovan sands, turned this county into the center of Alabama's onshore oil industry for a generation, and the Chunchula and Hatters Pond fields to the north kept drilling crews busy well after Citronelle's peak. What most owners don't know as precisely is what their own interest looks like today — whether it's still in a producing unit, whether the servitude or lease from a parent or grandparent ever lapsed, and what a current royalty check would actually support if someone made a fair offer.

The Alabama acquisition desk works as a family office buying mineral and royalty interests directly, and Mobile County is one of the places the Alabama acquisition desk spend the most time in the courthouse. The Probate Court in downtown Mobile holds the deed and probate records going back generations, and for anything touching the Citronelle trend the Alabama acquisition desk also cross-check unitization orders on file with the state. That's the work that has to happen before a number means anything, and the Alabama acquisition desk does it the Alabama acquisition desk rather than quoting off a map.

sections.title: The Citronelle Field and What Came After
sections.html:
Citronelle produced for decades on secondary and tertiary recovery long after the easy oil was gone, which means a lot of the mineral and royalty interests under the field have been held by production continuously since the 1950s. That's a meaningfully different situation from raw, undeveloped acreage — there's an actual production and payment history to underwrite. Chunchula and Hatters Pond, north and east of Citronelle, added their own layers of leasing activity through the 1970s and 1980s, and some of that acreage has been re-leased more than once as operators changed hands.

If your family's interest sits inside or near one of these fields, the practical question isn't whether the ground has ever produced — it almost certainly has, at some point — it's whether the well or unit paying you today is still economic, and how that shows up in the royalty statement you're currently getting, if you're getting one at all.

sections.title: Split Estates and Old Timber Land
sections.html:
A good share of Mobile County's rural acreage passed through large timber and land companies for much of the twentieth century, and a fair number of those companies severed the mineral estate from the surface before selling off the land. If your family bought or inherited surface ground in the county, there's a real chance you don't own what's under it — or the reverse, that a grandparent kept the minerals when the surface was sold and nobody since has tracked that reservation forward. Sorting out which side of that split you're on is exactly the kind of title question the Alabama acquisition desk runs down before the Alabama acquisition desk ever put a number in front of someone.

Heirs' property is common here too. Mobile County has a long history of land passing informally through families without a will, which leaves multiple cousins, siblings, or in-laws as tenants in common on the same mineral interest, sometimes without any of them realizing how many co-owners there actually are until a landman or buyer starts asking.

sections.title: What Actually Sets the Value
sections.html: Value on Mobile County minerals depends heavily on where the tract sits relative to Citronelle, Chunchula, and Hatters Pond, whether the unit is still producing or has watered out, and what the last several royalty checks actually show. The Alabama acquisition desk does not work off a flat county-wide number — a producing interest inside an active Citronelle unit and an unproven fraction on the county's edge are priced very differently, and both depend on current market activity, not a figure the Alabama acquisition desk quotes from memory.

sections.title: Probate Court Records and How the Alabama acquisition desk uses Them
sections.html: The Mobile County Probate Court holds the deed, conveyance, and probate books the Alabama acquisition desk pulls before making an offer, and for interests touching Citronelle the Alabama acquisition desk also checks the field's unitization and pooling orders with the state oil and gas board. That combination tells the Alabama acquisition desk what was actually conveyed, whether a later heir's transfer was ever recorded, and whether the interest as described on paper still matches what your family believes it owns. faqs.q: you think a great-grandparent sold the minerals when the timber company bought the land decades ago. How do you find out?

faqs.a: Not necessarily as a single transaction. Co-owners can sell individually or as a group, and the Alabama acquisition desk can structure an offer either way once the Alabama acquisition desk knows how the interest was actually divided among the heirs.

faqs.a: The Alabama acquisition desk does consider undeveloped acreage near active fields like Citronelle or Hatters Pond, though it's priced very differently than a producing royalty. Send the Alabama acquisition desk the details and the Alabama acquisition desk will give you an honest read on where it stands.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Baldwin County, AL
items.meta: Own oil and gas interests in Baldwin County, Alabama? Get a hedged, activity-based offer for minerals near Bay Minette, Daphne, Foley, or Elberta.

sections.html:
Baldwin County minerals sit on the quiet eastern edge of the Smackover-Norphlet fairway, and most of the parcels the Alabama acquisition desk reviews here trace back to a single family purchase generations ago.

Baldwin County is the largest county in Alabama by land area, and its mineral history is really two overlapping stories. Along the Mobile Bay shoreline and the interior pine flats near Bay Minette and Robertsdale, shallow gas and salt-dome structure extend eastward from the Mobile County core. Farther east and south, toward Foley and Elberta, oil and gas interest was leased more speculatively during the mid-century boom years and rarely developed, which is exactly why so many owners here still hold minerals they've never heard a word about since.

The Alabama acquisition desk works with families and individual owners across Baldwin County who inherited a fractional interest, found an old lease in a courthouse abstract, or simply want to convert a line item on a property tax bill into cash. This page walks through how minerals in Baldwin County are typically valued, what ownership tends to look like, and the questions the Alabama acquisition desk is asked most before a sale.

sections.title: Where Baldwin County sits in the play
sections.html:
Baldwin County borders the Mobile Bay side of the Norphlet and Smackover trend that produced the Citronelle Field in neighboring Mobile County and Jay Field along the Alabama-Florida line to the east. The county itself has seen far less drilling than either neighbor, but the same salt-dome and reef-trend geology underlies much of the western and southern county, which is why leasing activity has periodically picked up along the bay and near the Escambia County line without ever turning into sustained production for most tracts.

That history matters for value. A Baldwin County interest with no producing well nearby is priced very differently than one sitting inside an active drilling or spacing unit, and offers here are appropriately centered on lease-bonus comparables and permit activity rather than a royalty check history, since most owners in the county have never received one.

sections.title: How ownership usually looks here
sections.html:
Baldwin County's rapid growth along the Highway 59 and coastal corridors has pushed a lot of surface land into subdivisions, but mineral rights were commonly severed decades before that development and never followed the surface sale. It's routine for the Alabama acquisition desk to see a 40 or 80-acre mineral tract, sometimes reserved by a grandparent or great-grandparent who sold the surface but kept the minerals, now divided among a dozen or more heirs who may not even know the interest exists.

Because Baldwin County's probate court in Bay Minette handles the wills, estate filings, and heir determinations for property across the county, a title search there is usually the fastest way to confirm exactly who owns what percentage before any offer is finalized. If a prior owner died without a will, Alabama's intestate succession rules typically split the interest among children or, absent children, other next of kin, which is where tenancy-in-common ownership among cousins often originates.

sections.title: Split estate and non-participating interests
sections.html:
A meaningful share of the Baldwin County parcels the Alabama acquisition desk looks at are split estate, meaning the surface belongs to one owner (often a developer, farm, or timber operation today) while the mineral estate was reserved separately, sometimes generations ago. Others are non-participating royalty interests, where the owner is entitled to a royalty share if production ever occurs but has no right to sign a lease or negotiate bonus terms themselves.

Both situations are sellable, but the mechanics differ. A non-participating royalty interest is generally valued on a narrower set of comparables than a full mineral interest with executive rights, and the Alabama acquisition desk walks owners through which category their deed actually places them in before quoting anything.

sections.title: What the Alabama acquisition desk looks at before making an offer
sections.html:
For any Baldwin County tract, the Alabama acquisition desk pulls the county's current permit and leasing activity, check whether the parcel falls inside or near an established Alabama Oil and Gas Board field order, and review any prior lease history recorded at the courthouse. Interests near the Mobile County line or close to historic Norphlet-Smackover structure tend to carry a different range than interests in the county's eastern interior, where activity has been thinner.

From there the Alabama acquisition desk quotes a range tied to that activity rather than a flat number, and the Alabama acquisition desk is upfront when a specific tract is thinly traded, since an honest range beats a number the Alabama acquisition desk can't stand behind six months later.

faqs.q: you inherited part of a mineral interest in Baldwin County but you is not sure how much. Can you still make an offer?
faqs.a: Yes. The Alabama acquisition desk regularly works from a probate file or an old deed rather than a clean title report. The Alabama acquisition desk will help identify your fractional share as part of the process, and the offer is scaled to whatever percentage you can document.

faqs.q: There's no well on or near your Baldwin County land. Is the interest worth anything?
faqs.a: It can be, though the range is lower than for a producing tract and depends heavily on nearby permit activity and how close the parcel sits to the Norphlet-Smackover trend. The Alabama acquisition desk will tell you plainly if current activity doesn't support much of an offer.

faqs.q: your mineral interest is non-participating royalty, not a full mineral estate. Does that change anything?
faqs.a: It changes the valuation approach, not whether the Alabama acquisition desk can buy it. A non-participating royalty interest is priced on a different set of comparables since you don't hold executive rights, but it's still a sellable asset.

faqs.q: Do you need to hire an attorney before selling minerals in Baldwin County?
faqs.a: The Alabama acquisition desk is not attorneys and can't give legal advice, and for a straightforward inherited fractional interest most owners don't need one for the transaction itself. For complicated estates, unresolved probate, or disputes among heirs, talking to a local real estate or estate attorney first is worth the cost.

faqs.q: How long does closing usually take on a Baldwin County mineral sale?
faqs.a: Once ownership and acreage are confirmed against the county's records, most straightforward sales close within a few weeks. Estates still in active probate or interests split among many unlocated heirs take longer, since every owner's share has to be documented before closing.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Escambia County, AL
items.meta: Own mineral or royalty rights in Escambia County, Alabama, near the Jay Field Norphlet trend? Get a clear, patient cash offer on your interest.

sections.html:
Escambia County sits at the heart of Alabama's most productive onshore oil and gas trend, home to a piece of the Jay Field discovery and decades of Smackover and Norphlet development that make it one of the most consistently active counties in the state for mineral ownership.

If you hold a mineral or royalty interest in Escambia County, around Brewton, Flomaton, East Brewton, or the rural acreage between them, you are dealing with a genuinely active part of Alabama's oil and gas history, not a speculative fringe area. The Alabama acquisition desk evaluates these interests the way a family office looks at any real asset: understand the production, weigh the after-tax present value of holding against a lump sum today, and give you a straight answer either way.

This page walks through the geology, the courthouse realities, and what actually drives value here, so you know what to expect before you ever talk numbers with the Alabama acquisition desk.

sections.title: The Smackover and Norphlet story in Escambia County
sections.html:
Escambia County sits within the broader south Alabama extension of the Jurassic Smackover trend, a carbonate formation that has produced oil across the Gulf Coast for nearly a century, capped in places by the Norphlet sandstone, a gas-condensate reservoir that became a major exploration target once operators understood how to find it. The Jay Field discovery in 1970, straddling the Alabama-Florida line, was one of the largest Norphlet finds ever made and triggered a wave of leasing across this entire corner of the state.

Much of that trend is structurally controlled by salt movement, with the Smackover and Norphlet draped over and around ancient salt features that created the traps operators drilled into. That geology means production in Escambia County tends to be concentrated in specific structural highs rather than spread evenly across the county, so two tracts a few miles apart can have very different production histories depending on their position relative to these features.

Decades into development, most of this county's wells are mature. Production has declined substantially from the field's peak years, but a meaningful number of wells continue producing at lower, stripper-well volumes, generating steady if modest royalty checks for the mineral owners tied to them.

sections.title: Probate, heirs, and title work in Brewton
sections.html:
Brewton, the county seat, is where the Escambia County Probate Office holds deed, lease, and estate records for the entire county. Because heavy leasing activity in this area dates back to the early 1970s, a lot of the paperwork the Alabama acquisition desk deal with here is genuinely old, original lease agreements, early division orders, sometimes handwritten amendments, all of which the Alabama acquisition desk pulls and review before quoting.

Heirs' property and tenancy-in-common situations are common in this county, the same as in most of rural south Alabama. A tract leased fifty years ago has often passed through two or three generations since, sometimes without formal probate at every step. The Alabama acquisition desk can usually work with a properly executed heirship affidavit to establish your ownership without requiring a full, drawn-out probate proceeding, though every family's situation is different and the Alabama acquisition desk will tell you honestly what yours requires.

The Alabama acquisition desk can also purchase from individual heirs separately when a family co-owns an undivided interest and not everyone wants to sell at the same time.

sections.title: What actually moves the number on an Escambia County offer
sections.html:
Your net royalty decimal and recent production history matter most, but so does your tract's position relative to the historic Jay Field structure and any other locally productive units. An interest sitting within or near a well-documented producing area supports a stronger, more confident valuation than one on the trend's outer edge with a thinner history.

The Alabama acquisition desk also weigh the well's stage of decline. A stripper well late in its productive life behaves differently than one still on a steeper decline curve, and that shapes how the Alabama acquisition desk thinks about the present value of continuing to hold versus selling now. None of this is a fixed formula, it depends on your specific statements and current natural gas and condensate pricing, which is exactly why the Alabama acquisition desk asks to see your documentation before quoting a number rather than offering a blanket figure over the phone.

faqs.q: Is your Escambia County property actually part of the Jay Field trend?
faqs.a: Some tracts are within the historical field boundary or its Alabama extension, and some sit outside it; the Alabama acquisition desk checks your specific legal description against unit and production records to confirm.

faqs.q: Where are Escambia County's deed and probate records filed?
faqs.a: At the Escambia County Probate Office in Brewton, the county seat, which holds records for the entire county including Flomaton and East Brewton.

faqs.q: your family's lease dates back to the early 1970s Jay Field boom. Is it still valid?
faqs.a: It depends on whether production has continued to hold the lease; the Alabama acquisition desk researches the current well status tied to your specific agreement before answering.

faqs.q: What if the estate that passed this interest to you was never formally probated?
faqs.a: In many cases a signed heirship affidavit is enough to establish your ownership without full probate, though the Alabama acquisition desk reviews each situation individually to confirm what yours needs.

faqs.q: How does a mature, declining well affect what your interest is worth?
faqs.a: A well later in its decline typically has a lower but more predictable remaining production stream, which the Alabama acquisition desk factors into a valuation based on recent statements rather than the field's historical peak output.

faqs.q: Should you get tax advice before selling a mineral interest here?
faqs.a: It is worth understanding how a lump-sum sale compares to continued royalty income for your specific tax situation, and the Alabama acquisition desk encourages you to review that with your own CPA or tax advisor.

items.meta: Own mineral or royalty interests in Conecuh County, Alabama? Get a hedged, activity-based cash offer for land near Evergreen, Castleberry, or Repton.

sections.html:
Conecuh County sits on the flank of the Smackover-Norphlet trend that runs east from the old Citronelle discovery toward Jay Field, and the small legacy fields scattered through the county are the reason so many local families still hold minerals today.

Conecuh County's oil and gas history is quieter than Mobile or Escambia County's, but it isn't thin. The McKenzie Field and several smaller Smackover and Norphlet prospects sit inside county lines or just across the border in Monroe and Escambia counties, and leasing swept through much of rural Conecuh during the mid-century boom years that followed the 1955 Citronelle discovery. A lot of that leasing never produced a well, which is exactly why owners here so often have a mineral interest sitting quietly in a family estate with no royalty history attached to it at all.

Piney Woods farmland, timber tracts, and small family homesteads make up most of the county, and the mineral estate under that land was frequently severed from the surface decades ago, sometimes during a timber sale, sometimes reserved in a will. The Alabama acquisition desk buys those interests directly, and this page covers how Conecuh County minerals are typically valued, what ownership tends to look like on the ground, and the questions owners ask most before deciding to sell.

sections.title: Old leases and held-by-production questions
sections.html:
Because leasing in Conecuh County dates back decades in some places, a fair number of tracts carry an old lease that owners assume is still active. In most cases those leases lapsed long ago for lack of production or renewal, which restores full leasing rights to the mineral owner, but occasionally a lease was held by production from a small well that's still pumping quietly at a low rate.

Before the Alabama acquisition desk makes an offer, the Alabama acquisition desk checks the county's current well and permit status against any lease history in the courthouse abstract. If a well is actively producing on or near the tract, that materially changes the offer, since it means there's a real royalty stream to value rather than speculative acreage.

sections.title: Heirs' property and the county courthouse
sections.html:
Conecuh County, like much of rural south Alabama, has a real heirs'-property pattern. Land passed down informally across generations, without a will or a clean estate settlement, ends up owned by dozens of cousins as tenants in common, each holding an undivided fractional share. It's common for a single mineral tract here to trace back to one grandparent whose estate was never formally probated, leaving the current generation without clear individual deeds to their share.

The Conecuh County Probate Court in Evergreen is the starting point for sorting that out. Whether the record shows a formal probate, an affidavit of heirship, or nothing at all beyond an old handwritten will, the Alabama acquisition desk works from whatever documentation exists and help identify what percentage a given family member actually owns before quoting a number.

sections.title: What determines a fair range for a Conecuh County tract
sections.html:
The Alabama acquisition desk builds a range from recent permit filings, any producing wells within the relevant spacing unit, and comparable lease bonus or purchase activity the Alabama acquisition desk tracks across the Smackover-Norphlet trend in south Alabama, rather than quoting a flat number for the whole county. A parcel near the McKenzie Field boundary carries a different range than acreage on the county's less-tested northern edge, and the Alabama acquisition desk will explain which factors are driving the number the Alabama acquisition desk gives you.

The Alabama acquisition desk won't promise a specific dollar figure per acre before reviewing the tract, and the Alabama acquisition desk won't call an offer guaranteed, because activity in this part of Alabama moves with commodity prices and drilling budgets that shift year to year.

sections.title: Geology and the county's small legacy fields
sections.html:
Conecuh County lies along the eastern edge of the same Jurassic Smackover and Norphlet trend that produced the giant Citronelle Field to the west and Jay Field along the Florida line to the east. Between those two better-known fields, Conecuh has hosted smaller, scattered prospects, and permit activity here has always run in cycles tied to commodity prices rather than to any single sustained development program.

That pattern shapes how the Alabama acquisition desk looks at value. A tract inside or near a historic field boundary, with documented well control nearby, is priced differently than acreage in an untested part of the county, and the honest answer for a given parcel usually depends on what the state's permit and production records show for that specific township and range.

faqs.q: your family's Conecuh County land was never formally probated. Can you still sell the minerals?
faqs.a: Usually, yes, but every heir with a legal interest generally needs to be identified and sign off. The Alabama acquisition desk works from affidavits of heirship, old wills, or whatever partial documentation exists, and the Alabama acquisition desk will walk you through what's needed to move forward.

faqs.q: There's an old lease on file for your land from decades ago. Is it still binding?
faqs.a: Most leases from that era expired long ago if no well was drilled or production stopped, which returns full leasing rights to you. The Alabama acquisition desk checks the current status against county and state permit records before making an offer so you know exactly where things stand.

faqs.q: How does Conecuh County compare to Mobile or Escambia County for mineral value?
faqs.a: Conecuh generally sees less well control and thinner activity than the Citronelle or Jay Field cores, so ranges here tend to run lower, though tracts near the McKenzie Field or other documented prospects can still carry real value. The Alabama acquisition desk prices against recent activity in your specific area rather than a countywide average.

sections.html:
Monroe County sits in the quieter stretch of Alabama's south-state oil country, between the Citronelle trend to the west and the Smackover tests that have worked their way through this part of the state for decades.

Monroe County doesn't get talked about the way Mobile or Escambia County does, but families here have held mineral and royalty interests for generations, often tied to leasing activity that swept through south Alabama in waves — a round in the 1950s and 1960s chasing shallower production, and later rounds testing deeper Jurassic-age Smackover and Norphlet targets as operators pushed further to find what the Citronelle Field had already proven was possible nearby. Most of what the Alabama acquisition desk sees in this county is older acreage, passed down through two or three generations, where the current owner has a vague sense that “there's oil and gas under there somewhere” but no clear picture of what's actually leased, what's producing, or what any of it is worth today.

The Alabama acquisition desk buys mineral and royalty interests directly, and in Monroe County that starts with the courthouse in Monroeville, the county seat. Before the Alabama acquisition desk quotes anyone a number, the Alabama acquisition desk pulls the conveyance and probate books the Alabama acquisition desk to see what was actually conveyed, whether the mineral estate was ever severed from the surface, and how many heirs the interest has passed through since the original owner held it.

sections.title: Scattered Leasing Waves Instead of One Big Field
sections.html:
Unlike Mobile County, which has one dominant field defining most of its production history, Monroe County's oil and gas story is more scattered — exploratory leasing that came and went as operators tested different formations at different depths. That pattern means ownership here is genuinely mixed: some tracts sit near wells with real production history, others were leased decades ago, tested, and never drilled, and a fair number were leased, held for a primary term, and simply released back to the mineral owner without anyone telling the family what that meant.

If your interest has never produced, that doesn't make it worthless, but it does mean the conversation about value has to start with the lease and title history rather than a royalty statement, because there may not be one.

sections.title: Heirs' Property and Tenancy in Common
sections.html:
Monroe County has a lot of rural land that passed through families without formal wills, which is exactly how heirs' property situations develop — a mineral interest ends up owned by a shifting group of siblings, cousins, and in-laws as tenants in common, often without a clean paper trail connecting the current generation back to the original grantee. The Alabama acquisition desk sees this constantly in this county specifically, and it's usually the single biggest thing slowing a sale down, more than the geology.

Untangling it starts with the probate file for whichever ancestor last held clear title, then working forward through each subsequent estate. It's tedious, but it's necessary, and the Alabama acquisition desk does that work the Alabama acquisition desk rather than asking a family to hire a title attorney before the Alabama acquisition desk will even talk.

sections.title: Split Estate From Old Timber and Turpentine Land
sections.html: A meaningful share of Monroe County's rural land moved through timber companies in the early and mid-twentieth century, some of it originally tied to the turpentine and naval stores industry that worked this part of Alabama before large-scale pulpwood took over. Those transactions frequently severed the mineral estate from the surface, which means plenty of families who own the surface today don't own what's under it, and the reverse is just as common — a family that sold the surface generations ago but kept the minerals, unaware that those minerals still have value independent of the land itself.

sections.title: What the Alabama acquisition desk looks At Before Making an Offer
sections.html: Value in Monroe County depends on proximity to whatever leasing or drilling activity has occurred nearby, whether the tract has ever been included in a producing unit, and — for interests that have produced — what recent royalty checks actually show. The Alabama acquisition desk prices against that real, current information, not a flat per-acre number pulled from a neighboring parish or county, because activity in south Alabama varies block by block, not county by county.

faqs.q: your grandfather's lease from decades ago expired with no well drilled. Do you still own the minerals?

faqs.q: How is Monroe County different from the bigger oil counties nearby?
faqs.a: There's no single dominant field here the way Citronelle defines Mobile County. Activity has come in scattered leasing waves, so value depends much more on the specific tract's history than on the county as a whole.

sections.html:
Citronelle is the name on Alabama's most significant oil discovery, a field that once ranked as the largest producing onshore field east of the Mississippi River, and mineral ownership here carries more documented history than almost anywhere else in the state.

Discovered in 1955, Citronelle Field tapped the Rodessa and Donovan sands at depths beyond 10,000 feet, kicking off a leasing and drilling rush that touched nearly every tract in and around the town. Decades later, after primary production declined, the field saw a second life through CO2 enhanced oil recovery, injecting carbon dioxide to push additional oil toward existing wellbores. Owners here are more likely than in almost any other Alabama town to have an actual royalty history, though the character of that history varies enormously from one tract to the next depending on where it sits relative to the field's productive core.

sections.title: Two generations of production
sections.html: Citronelle's original primary production phase ran for decades before naturally declining, and the field was later redeveloped for CO2 flooding, a process that reworks existing reservoirs rather than requiring new discovery. That means some tracts here have two distinct royalty histories to review, an original production run and a later secondary or tertiary recovery phase, each with its own decline pattern.

sections.title: Where your tract sits matters enormously
sections.html: Because Citronelle Field covers a defined structural area rather than the whole town uniformly, a parcel inside the field's mapped productive limits is valued very differently than one on the surrounding periphery that was leased during the boom years but never actually produced. The Alabama acquisition desk checks Alabama Oil and Gas Board field records against your specific legal description before quoting.

sections.title: What the Alabama acquisition desk reviews for a Citronelle interest

For peripheral acreage with lease history but no production, the Alabama acquisition desk builds a range from comparable bonus and permit activity instead.

faqs.a: It sits outside the most heavily developed part of the fairway, closer to Oak Grove and Brookwood, so the Alabama acquisition desk typically prices interests here as speculative acreage rather than active producing royalty.

faqs.q: your deed mentions an old coal company that doesn't exist anymore. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: No, that's common with older Woodstock-area land. The Alabama acquisition desk is experienced tracing chains of title through successor entities and county probate records even when the original company name is unfamiliar.

faqs.q: Should you check whether your parcel is actually in Bibb County instead of Tuscaloosa County?
faqs.a: It's worth confirming since Woodstock sits near the line. Your deed's legal description will show the county, and the Alabama acquisition desk can verify it as part of the Alabama acquisition desk's review if you're unsure.

items.name: Got an Unsolicited Offer?
items.meta: A letter showed up offering to buy your Alabama mineral rights. Before you sign anything, see how to benchmark that offer against what the interest is actually worth.

sections.html:
A letter arrives out of nowhere offering to buy your mineral rights, with a number attached and a deadline that makes it sound like this is your only chance, and that framing alone should be the first thing that gives you pause.

Unsolicited mineral offers are a normal part of owning Alabama mineral rights, and they are not automatically a scam. Legitimate buyers do send cold offers, sometimes because public leasing or permitting activity flagged your county as one worth pursuing. But an offer arriving unprompted, with pressure to respond quickly and no real explanation of how the number was reached, is exactly the situation where getting a second opinion before signing matters most.

The Alabama acquisition desk benchmarks unsolicited offers for owners all the time, at no cost and with no obligation to sell to the Alabama acquisition desk. If the Alabama acquisition desk's number comes in close to what you already have in hand, that is useful confirmation. If it comes in meaningfully higher, that is worth knowing before you sign anything away.

sections.title: Why Cold Offers Are Often Priced Low
sections.html:
A buyer sending mail offers to a large list of owners across a county is typically working from public records and general area assumptions, not your specific production history, decline curve, or operator. That approach tends to produce a conservative number aimed at owners who will not check further, and it is not necessarily a bad-faith number, just an efficient one for the buyer's process rather than one tailored to your interest.

The Alabama acquisition desk builds the Alabama acquisition desk's numbers from your actual documentation whenever you can provide it: recent check stubs, a division order, or even just the well name if you know it. That specificity is usually what separates a benchmarked, informed offer from a generic mailer.

sections.title: Questions Worth Asking Before You Sign Anything
sections.html:
Ask what the offer is based on. If the answer is vague, that is telling. Ask whether the deadline is real or manufactured, since a genuinely fair offer does not usually depend on you signing within 48 hours. Ask whether the buyer is purchasing the mineral interest outright or something else entirely, like an option or a lease, since the language in these mailers is not always as straightforward as it reads.

It is also worth checking whether the offer covers your full interest or only a portion, and whether it references the correct legal description and county for what you actually own. The Alabama acquisition desk sees mismatches here more often than owners expect.

sections.title: Getting a Second Number Costs You Nothing
sections.html: Send the Alabama acquisition desk the offer along with whatever ownership documentation you have, and the Alabama acquisition desk will give you the Alabama acquisition desk's own honest read on whether it looks fair, low, or generous, based on the same production and title factors any serious buyer should be using. There is no obligation to sell to the Alabama acquisition desk, and no cost to ask. Owners who take this step before signing rarely regret the extra day or two it takes.

sections.title: What a Genuinely Competitive Process Looks Like
sections.html:
If you have received one unsolicited offer, it is reasonable to assume you could receive others, since buyers working the same county records often send letters to overlapping owner lists. Rather than accepting the first number, some owners choose to solicit a second or third opinion deliberately, which can be as simple as reaching out to a couple of buyers with the same documentation and comparing what comes back.

The Alabama acquisition desk is comfortable being one of several offers you gather rather than insisting on exclusivity, and the Alabama acquisition desk would rather earn your business on a fair number than on being the only option you considered.

faqs.q: Should you get multiple offers before selling to anyone?
faqs.a: It is a reasonable approach, and the Alabama acquisition desk is comfortable being one of several offers you compare. A fair number should hold up against competing quotes, not depend on being your only option.

faqs.q: Is an unsolicited mineral rights offer usually a scam?
faqs.a: Not usually, most are legitimate buyers, but the offer is often priced conservatively since it is not based on your specific production history. Verifying it before signing is simply good practice.

faqs.q: Will you charge you to review an offer you already received?
faqs.a: No. Benchmarking an offer against the Alabama acquisition desk's own valuation is free and comes with no obligation to sell to the Alabama acquisition desk instead.

faqs.q: The offer has a short deadline. Should you feel rushed?
faqs.a: A genuinely fair offer does not typically depend on an artificial deadline. A short fuse is a reason to slow down and verify, not a reason to sign quickly.

faqs.q: What documents should you send you to benchmark an offer?
faqs.a: The offer letter itself, along with any deed, division order, or recent check stub you have. The more documentation you can provide, the more precise the Alabama acquisition desk's read on the offer will be.

faqs.q: The letter says the offer expires in a set number of days. Is that normal?
faqs.a: Some buyers do use time-limited offers as standard practice, but a legitimate one should still hold up to scrutiny. If a deadline is being used to discourage you from checking the number, treat that as a warning sign.

faqs.q: Can you negotiate the number in an unsolicited offer, or is it take it or leave it?
faqs.a: Most offers are negotiable, particularly once you provide documentation the original buyer did not have. A benchmarked counteroffer backed by your own records is often the most effective way to negotiate.

items.name: Inherited Mineral Rights
items.meta: Just inherited Alabama mineral or royalty interests? Learn how heirs typically decide whether to keep, lease, or sell, and what a fair valuation actually looks like.

sections.html:
Inheriting a mineral interest usually arrives with more questions than paperwork, starting with what exactly it is you now own and whether keeping it makes sense for your life rather than the one your parents or grandparents lived.

Mineral rights in Alabama get passed down differently than most inherited assets. There is rarely a single clean statement of value the way there is with a brokerage account, and the interest itself may be producing, leased but idle, or sitting completely dormant with no activity in years. Heirs often discover the interest exists only when a royalty check with an unfamiliar company name shows up, or when an attorney mentions it during probate almost as an afterthought.

The Alabama acquisition desk's job when someone inherits is to help them understand what they actually hold before they decide anything. Sometimes that conversation ends with an owner deciding to keep the interest and collect royalties long-term. Just as often, it ends with a decision to sell, because the interest does not fit how that person wants to manage their own financial life.

sections.title: Understanding What You Actually Inherited
sections.html:
The first step is simply confirming what type of interest passed to you. A mineral interest, a royalty interest, and a working interest carry very different obligations and very different risk, and the deed or will language does not always spell that out in plain terms. The Alabama acquisition desk reviews whatever documents you have and, where needed, pull the recorded instruments the Alabama acquisition desk to confirm exactly what you hold and where it sits.

It also matters whether the interest is currently producing, leased with a bonus already paid but no drilling yet, or dormant with no lease at all. Each of those has a different value profile, and heirs are frequently surprised to learn theirs falls into a category different from what a relative told them growing up.

sections.title: The Case for Keeping It
sections.html:
If the interest is actively producing with a reasonably stable royalty history, and you are comfortable managing the annual tax reporting and occasional division order updates that come with ownership, holding onto it as a long-term income stream can make sense for some families. The Alabama acquisition desk never pushes an owner toward selling who would genuinely rather keep collecting checks.

The honest tradeoff is that oil and gas royalties decline over time as wells deplete, and value depends heavily on commodity pricing that is outside anyone's control. An interest worth keeping today is not guaranteed to look the same in ten years.

sections.title: The Case for Selling
sections.html:
Many heirs, especially those who live out of state or inherited alongside siblings, decide that converting the interest into a single lump sum is simpler than managing a small, unpredictable income stream indefinitely, particularly one they did not choose to acquire in the first place. A sale also resolves any future disagreement among co-heirs about leasing decisions or eventual sale timing.

The Alabama acquisition desk builds the Alabama acquisition desk's offer from the interest's actual production history and current lease status rather than a flat number by county, and the Alabama acquisition desk walks you through exactly how that figure was calculated before you decide anything.

sections.title: When Several Siblings Inherit the Same Interest
sections.html:
It is common for a single mineral interest to pass to multiple children or grandchildren at once, each receiving an undivided fractional share. That arrangement works fine when everyone agrees on what to do, but it can create real friction when one sibling wants to keep collecting royalties and another wants to sell and move on. Alabama law generally lets each co-owner decide independently for their own share, which means the family does not need unanimous agreement before anyone can act.

The Alabama acquisition desk regularly buys one sibling's share while others retain theirs, and the Alabama acquisition desk can also coordinate a single closing for everyone who does want to sell, which tends to simplify the title work since all the shares trace back to the same original deed or estate.

faqs.q: your siblings and you disagree about selling. What are your options?
faqs.a: You generally control your own undivided share independent of what your siblings decide. The Alabama acquisition desk can purchase your portion alone while others keep theirs, or coordinate a joint closing if everyone agrees.

faqs.q: Do you need to finish probate before you can sell an inherited mineral interest?
faqs.a: Generally yes, title needs to be cleared and recorded in the heir's name, or the estate needs authority to sell, before a purchase can close. The Alabama acquisition desk can start valuation work in parallel while probate finishes.

faqs.q: How do you find out if your inherited interest is even producing?
faqs.a: The Alabama acquisition desk can research the property using the county and legal description from the deed or will, and identify the current operator and recent activity even if you have never received a check.
